course.title: SQL Masterclass
course.tagline: Zero to advanced, one module at a time.
course.standard: PostgreSQL-first, with MySQL, SQLite and SQL Server notes.
course.description: Module 11 teaches scalar, multi-row, correlated and EXISTS subqueries, derived tables, HAVING subqueries, CTEs, recursive CTEs and data-modifying CTEs.
outcomes: Use EXISTS and NOT EXISTS safely
Use derived tables and HAVING subqueries

modules.title: Subqueries and CTEs
modules.goal: Break complex questions into correct, readable subqueries and CTEs.

topics.title: Introduction to Subqueries
topics.simple: Subquery ek query ke andar doosri query hoti hai.
topics.pro: A subquery is a SELECT nested inside another statement; it can supply a value, a row set or an existence test.
points: They run in the context of the outer query.
They can appear in SELECT, FROM, WHERE and HAVING.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students);

topics.title: Types of Subqueries
topics.simple: Subquery scalar, multi-row ya correlated ho sakti hai.
topics.pro: Subqueries are classified by shape (scalar or multi-row) and by dependency (uncorrelated or correlated).

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments);
example.output: Students with at least one enrollment.

topics.title: Scalar Subquery
topics.simple: Scalar subquery ek row aur ek column deti hai.
topics.pro: A scalar subquery returns exactly one row and one column, so it can be used anywhere a single value is accepted.

example.sql: SELECT name, (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students) AS class_average FROM students;
example.output: Every student with the same class average.

topics.title: Multi-row Subquery
topics.simple: Multi-row subquery multiple values deti hai; IN ya ANY/ALL ke saath use karo.
topics.pro: A multi-row subquery returns one column with many rows and is compared with IN, ANY or ALL rather than a plain equality.
points: A plain = with many rows fails.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10);

topics.title: Correlated Subquery
topics.simple: Correlated subquery outer query ke row par depend karti hai.
topics.pro: A correlated subquery references a column from the outer query, so conceptually it is evaluated for each outer row.
points: It can be expensive without an index.
It is often rewritten as a join.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id) AS courses FROM students s;
example.output: Each student with their enrollment count.

topics.title: Subquery in WHERE
topics.simple: WHERE me subquery se filter value ya set deti hai.
topics.pro: A subquery in WHERE can compare a column to a scalar or test membership and existence.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students);

topics.title: Subquery with IN
topics.simple: IN subquery ke result set me membership check karta hai.
topics.pro: IN tests whether a value equals any row returned by the subquery, and handles a multi-row result naturally.
points: NULLs in the list can make NOT IN unsafe.
Duplicates in the subquery do not duplicate output.

example.sql: SELECT name FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10);
example.output: Students enrolled in course 10, once each.

topics.title: Subquery with EXISTS
topics.simple: EXISTS subquery ke row hone par true hota hai.
topics.pro: EXISTS returns true as soon as the subquery produces at least one row; the selected columns are irrelevant and the planner can stop early.
points: It can short-circuit on the first match.

example.sql: SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id);
example.output: Students with at least one enrollment.

topics.title: Subquery with NOT EXISTS
topics.simple: NOT EXISTS tab true hota hai jab subquery koi row na de.
topics.pro: NOT EXISTS returns true when the correlated subquery produces no rows, making it a safe anti-join even with NULLs.
points: It usually beats NOT IN with nullable columns.

example.sql: SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id);

topics.title: Subquery in SELECT
topics.simple: SELECT list me scalar subquery ek computed column deti hai.
topics.pro: A scalar subquery in the select list computes one value per output row and must return at most one row and one column.
points: It runs per outer row when correlated.
It can be expensive on large results.

example.sql: SELECT s.name, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id) AS courses FROM students s;

topics.title: Subquery in FROM
topics.simple: FROM me subquery derived table ki tarah use hoti hai.
topics.pro: A subquery in FROM acts as a derived table and must have an alias in PostgreSQL; its columns are then queried like a normal table.
points: It can aggregate before the outer query.
It is often called a derived table.

example.sql: SELECT t.course_id, t.total FROM (SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id) AS t WHERE t.total > 1;
example.output: Courses with more than one enrollment.

topics.title: Subquery in HAVING
topics.simple: HAVING me subquery aggregate result se compare kar sakti hai.
topics.pro: A subquery in HAVING supplies a scalar threshold or value after grouping, which is useful for comparing groups to a global aggregate.

example.sql: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(*) > (SELECT AVG(cnt) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id) AS x);
example.output: Courses above the average enrollment count.

topics.title: Introduction to CTEs
topics.simple: CTE WITH clause se named temporary result set banata hai.
topics.pro: A common table expression is a named subquery defined with WITH and visible to the statement that follows it.
points: It is scoped to one statement.

example.sql: WITH high AS (SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > 80) SELECT * FROM high ORDER BY marks DESC;

topics.title: CTE Syntax
topics.simple: WITH name AS (query) SELECT ... .
topics.pro: The syntax is WITH name [(columns)] AS (subquery) [, ...] SELECT ...; the CTE can be referenced like a table in the main query.

example.sql: WITH avg_marks AS (SELECT AVG(marks) AS avg FROM students) SELECT name FROM students, avg_marks WHERE marks > avg;

topics.title: Multiple CTEs
topics.simple: Ek WITH me comma se multiple CTEs define karo.
topics.pro: Multiple CTEs are separated by commas and later CTEs can reference earlier ones, which lets a complex query read top to bottom.

example.sql: WITH high AS (SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 80), count_high AS (SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM high) SELECT * FROM count_high;

topics.title: Recursive CTE
topics.simple: Recursive CTE anchor aur recursive term se hierarchy ya sequence banata hai.
topics.pro: WITH RECURSIVE runs an anchor term, then repeatedly runs a recursive term that references the CTE until it returns no rows.
points: The recursive term needs a termination condition.

example.sql: WITH RECURSIVE nums AS (SELECT 1 AS n UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM nums WHERE n < 5) SELECT * FROM nums;

topics.title: CTE vs Subquery
topics.simple: CTE named aur reusable hai; subquery inline hoti hai.
topics.pro: A CTE names a result for readability and reuse within one statement, while a subquery is inline; PostgreSQL may inline a non-recursive CTE unless MATERIALIZED is specified.
points: CTEs can be referenced multiple times.
Subqueries are local to their expression.

example.sql: WITH avg_marks AS (SELECT AVG(marks) AS avg FROM students) SELECT name FROM students, avg_marks WHERE marks > avg;

topics.title: CTE with DML
topics.simple: PostgreSQL me CTE ke andar INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE chal sakta hai.
topics.pro: A data-modifying CTE uses RETURNING to expose changed rows to the main query; the statement executes once and is atomic.
points: DML CTEs need RETURNING to expose rows.

example.sql: WITH deleted AS (DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60 RETURNING *) SELECT * FROM deleted;

topics.title: Common Subquery Errors
topics.simple: Multi-row scalar, missing alias aur NULL NOT IN sabse common errors hain.
topics.pro: Common failures are a scalar subquery returning multiple rows, a derived table without an alias, a missing correlation condition and NOT IN with NULLs.
points: Prefer NOT EXISTS over NOT IN.

example.sql: SELECT name, (SELECT marks FROM students LIMIT 1) AS sample FROM students;
example.output: A single sample mark per row.

topics.title: Performance Considerations
topics.simple: Subqueries hamesha slow nahi hoti; shape aur indexes matter karte hain.
topics.pro: EXISTS can short-circuit, correlated subqueries can run per row, and CTE materialization can help or hurt; read EXPLAIN instead of guessing.
points: EXISTS often stops at the first match.
CTEs may be inlined or materialized.

example.sql: EXPLAIN SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id);
example.output: A plan showing a semi-join or nested loop.

learn.q: What is a subquery?
options: A query nested inside another statement
learn.answer: A query nested inside another statement
learn.why: It supplies a value or row set to the outer query.

learn.q: What does a scalar subquery return?
learn.why: A scalar is a single value.

learn.q: What does a multi-row subquery return?
learn.why: It is used with IN, ANY or ALL.

learn.q: What makes a subquery correlated?
learn.why: It depends on the current outer row.

learn.q: Which operator tests membership in a subquery result?
learn.why: IN compares against a set of values.

learn.q: What does EXISTS test?
options: Whether the subquery returns any row
learn.answer: Whether the subquery returns any row
learn.why: EXISTS is a boolean existence test.

learn.q: What does NOT EXISTS test?
options: Whether the subquery returns no rows
Whether a column is NOT NULL
learn.answer: Whether the subquery returns no rows
learn.why: It is the safe anti-join.

learn.q: Where can a scalar subquery appear?
learn.why: Anywhere a single value is accepted.

learn.q: What must a subquery in FROM have?
learn.why: PostgreSQL requires a derived-table alias.

learn.q: Which clause filters groups using an aggregate?
learn.why: HAVING runs after grouping.

learn.q: What does WITH define?
learn.why: WITH names a subquery for the statement.

learn.q: How are multiple CTEs separated?
learn.why: WITH a AS (...), b AS (...) ... .

learn.q: Which keyword enables a recursive CTE?
learn.why: WITH RECURSIVE allows self-reference.

learn.q: What are the two parts of a recursive CTE?
learn.why: The anchor seeds the result; the recursive term expands it.

learn.q: What terminates a recursive CTE?
options: A condition that eventually returns no rows
learn.answer: A condition that eventually returns no rows
learn.why: Without termination it runs until cancelled.

learn.q: How does a CTE differ from a subquery?
options: It is named and reusable in the statement
learn.answer: It is named and reusable in the statement
learn.why: A CTE can be referenced more than once.

learn.q: Which clause exposes changed rows from a DML CTE?
learn.why: RETURNING makes the changed rows available to the main query.

learn.q: What error does a multi-row scalar subquery raise?
learn.why: A scalar slot cannot hold multiple rows.

learn.q: Why is NOT IN unsafe with NULLs?
options: NULL comparisons make the predicate unknown
learn.answer: NULL comparisons make the predicate unknown
learn.why: A NULL in the list can make NOT IN return no rows.

learn.q: Which is usually the safer anti-join?
learn.why: NOT EXISTS handles NULLs predictably.

interview.answer: A SELECT nested inside another statement, used for a scalar value, a row set or an existence test.
A subquery returning at most one row and one column, usable as a single value.
A subquery returning one column with many rows, used with IN, ANY or ALL.
A subquery that references a column from the outer query and depends on the current outer row.
A subquery that can be evaluated independently of the outer query.

interview.q: What is the difference between IN and EXISTS?
interview.answer: IN compares a value to a set; EXISTS tests whether any row exists and can short-circuit.

interview.q: Why is NOT EXISTS safer than NOT IN?
interview.answer: NOT EXISTS handles NULLs predictably; NOT IN with a NULL can return no rows.
A subquery in FROM with an alias, queried like a table by the outer query.

interview.q: Why does a FROM subquery need an alias?
interview.answer: PostgreSQL requires a name for the derived relation so its columns can be referenced.
A named subquery defined with WITH and visible to the statement that follows.

interview.q: What are the advantages of a CTE?
interview.answer: Readability, reuse within one statement and a clean way to structure multi-step queries.
A CTE with an anchor term and a recursive term that references itself until no more rows are produced.
The non-recursive seed query that starts the recursive result.

interview.q: What happens if a recursive CTE has no termination condition?
interview.answer: It keeps producing rows until the statement is cancelled or a resource limit is hit.
A CTE containing INSERT, UPDATE or DELETE with RETURNING, whose rows the main query can read.

interview.q: How many times does a data-modifying CTE execute?
interview.answer: Exactly once, even if the main query references it multiple times.

interview.q: Does a CTE create a temporary table?
interview.answer: No; it is a named query scoped to one statement.

interview.q: Are CTEs always materialized in PostgreSQL?
interview.answer: No; since PostgreSQL 12 non-recursive CTEs can be inlined, and MATERIALIZED / NOT MATERIALIZED can control it.
A join that returns rows from one side when a match exists, without duplicating them for every match; EXISTS is a common form.

interview.q: How do you performance-tune a correlated subquery?
interview.answer: Index the correlated columns, compare with an EXISTS or join rewrite, and inspect EXPLAIN ANALYZE.

labs.title: Scalar average
labs.task: Return students above the class average.
labs.solution: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks > (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students);

labs.title: IN subquery
labs.task: Return students enrolled in course 10.
labs.solution: SELECT name FROM students WHERE id IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments WHERE course_id = 10);

labs.title: ANY subquery
labs.task: Return students whose marks equal any applicant mark.
labs.solution: SELECT name FROM students WHERE marks = ANY (SELECT marks FROM applicants);

labs.title: EXISTS
labs.task: Return students with at least one enrollment.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id);

labs.title: NOT EXISTS
labs.task: Return students with no enrollments.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id);

labs.title: Correlated count
labs.task: Return each student with their enrollment count.
labs.solution: SELECT s.name, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id) AS courses FROM students s;

labs.title: Subquery in SELECT
labs.task: Return the class average on every row.
labs.solution: SELECT name, (SELECT AVG(marks) FROM students) AS class_average FROM students;
labs.expected: Every student with the same average.

labs.title: Derived table
labs.task: Return courses with more than one enrollment.
labs.solution: SELECT t.course_id, t.total FROM (SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id) AS t WHERE t.total > 1;

labs.title: Subquery in HAVING
labs.task: Return courses above the average enrollment count.
labs.solution: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(*) > (SELECT AVG(cnt) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id) AS x);

labs.title: Basic CTE
labs.task: Return high scorers using a CTE.
labs.solution: WITH high AS (SELECT name, marks FROM students WHERE marks > 80) SELECT * FROM high ORDER BY marks DESC;

labs.title: Multiple CTEs
labs.task: Count the high scorers using two CTEs.
labs.solution: WITH high AS (SELECT * FROM students WHERE marks > 80), count_high AS (SELECT COUNT(*) AS n FROM high) SELECT * FROM count_high;

labs.title: Recursive numbers
labs.task: Generate 1 through 5 with a recursive CTE.
labs.solution: WITH RECURSIVE nums AS (SELECT 1 AS n UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM nums WHERE n < 5) SELECT * FROM nums;

labs.title: Recursive hierarchy
labs.task: Return employees and their manager names.
labs.solution: WITH RECURSIVE chain AS (SELECT id, name, manager_id FROM employees WHERE manager_id IS NULL UNION ALL SELECT e.id, e.name, e.manager_id FROM employees e JOIN chain c ON e.manager_id = c.id) SELECT * FROM chain;
labs.expected: The hierarchy from the root down.

labs.title: DML CTE delete
labs.task: Delete low marks and return the deleted rows.
labs.solution: WITH deleted AS (DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60 RETURNING *) SELECT * FROM deleted;

labs.title: DML CTE update
labs.task: Raise low marks and return the updated rows.
labs.solution: WITH updated AS (UPDATE students SET marks = marks + 5 WHERE marks < 60 RETURNING *) SELECT * FROM updated;

labs.title: CTE vs subquery
labs.task: Rewrite the average filter as a CTE.
labs.solution: WITH avg_marks AS (SELECT AVG(marks) AS avg FROM students) SELECT name FROM students, avg_marks WHERE marks > avg;

labs.title: Materialized CTE
labs.task: Force the average CTE to materialize.
labs.solution: WITH avg_marks AS MATERIALIZED (SELECT AVG(marks) AS avg FROM students) SELECT name FROM students, avg_marks WHERE marks > avg;

labs.title: Explain EXISTS
labs.task: Explain the enrolled-students query.
labs.solution: EXPLAIN SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id);

labs.title: Top course count
labs.task: Return courses with the maximum enrollment count.
labs.solution: SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id HAVING COUNT(*) = (SELECT MAX(cnt) FROM (SELECT COUNT(*) AS cnt FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id) AS x);

labs.title: Report with CTEs
labs.task: Build a course enrollment report with a CTE.
labs.solution: WITH counts AS (SELECT course_id, COUNT(*) AS total FROM enrollments GROUP BY course_id) SELECT c.title, counts.total FROM courses c JOIN counts ON counts.course_id = c.id ORDER BY counts.total DESC;

logic.answer: When it can run independently of the outer query and returns the same result for every outer row.

logic.q: Why can a correlated subquery be slower?
logic.answer: It may run once per outer row, so missing indexes multiply the work.
It only needs one matching row to return true.

logic.q: Why is NOT IN dangerous with NULLs?
logic.answer: A NULL comparison is unknown, so the predicate can fail for every row.

logic.q: Why does a scalar subquery fail with multiple rows?
logic.answer: A single-value slot cannot represent more than one row.

logic.q: Why must a FROM subquery have an alias?
logic.answer: The outer query needs a relation name to qualify its columns.

logic.q: Why use a CTE instead of a nested subquery?
logic.answer: A CTE names each step and can be referenced multiple times, improving readability and reuse.

logic.q: Why can a CTE hurt performance?
logic.answer: Materializing a large intermediate result can cost more than letting the planner inline and optimize the query.

logic.q: Why can MATERIALIZED change a plan?
logic.answer: It forces the CTE result to be computed once instead of being inlined into the outer query.

logic.q: Why does a recursive CTE need an anchor?
logic.answer: The anchor produces the starting rows; the recursive term expands from them.

logic.q: Why does a recursive CTE need a termination condition?
logic.answer: Without one it keeps producing rows until cancelled or limited.

logic.q: Why is a CTE scoped to one statement?
logic.answer: It is a named query, not a persistent table, and disappears when the statement ends.

logic.q: Why does a data-modifying CTE execute once?
logic.answer: The statement runs the CTE once even if the main query references its output repeatedly.

logic.q: Why can a subquery in SELECT be expensive?
logic.answer: A correlated scalar subquery may execute for every output row.

logic.q: Why prefer EXISTS over IN for existence checks?
logic.answer: EXISTS expresses the intent directly and can short-circuit on the first match.

debug.title: Scalar returns many rows
debug.broken: SELECT name, (SELECT marks FROM students) AS sample FROM students;
debug.fix: SELECT name, (SELECT marks FROM students LIMIT 1) AS sample FROM students;
debug.error: more than one row returned by a subquery used as an expression

debug.title: Missing derived alias
debug.fix: SELECT * FROM (SELECT name FROM students) AS s;
debug.error: subquery in FROM must have an alias

debug.title: Correlation missing
debug.broken: SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e);
debug.fix: SELECT s.name FROM students s WHERE EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id);
debug.error: Every student is returned when any enrollment exists
debug.expected: Only students with a matching enrollment.

debug.title: NOT IN with NULL
debug.broken: SELECT name FROM students WHERE id NOT IN (SELECT student_id FROM enrollments);
debug.fix: SELECT name FROM students s WHERE NOT EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id);
debug.error: A NULL student_id can make the result empty

debug.title: Recursive without termination
debug.broken: WITH RECURSIVE nums AS (SELECT 1 AS n UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM nums) SELECT * FROM nums;
debug.fix: WITH RECURSIVE nums AS (SELECT 1 AS n UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM nums WHERE n < 5) SELECT * FROM nums;

debug.title: Recursive keyword missing
debug.broken: WITH nums AS (SELECT 1 AS n UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM nums WHERE n < 5) SELECT * FROM nums;
debug.fix: WITH RECURSIVE nums AS (SELECT 1 AS n UNION ALL SELECT n + 1 FROM nums WHERE n < 5) SELECT * FROM nums;

debug.title: Duplicate CTE name
debug.broken: WITH x AS (SELECT 1), x AS (SELECT 2) SELECT * FROM x;
debug.fix: WITH x AS (SELECT 1), y AS (SELECT 2) SELECT * FROM x;
debug.error: WITH query name "x" specified more than once

debug.title: ORDER BY in a subquery
debug.broken: SELECT * FROM (SELECT name FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC) AS s;
debug.fix: SELECT * FROM (SELECT name FROM students ORDER BY marks DESC LIMIT 3) AS s;
debug.error: The inner ORDER BY is not guaranteed to survive

debug.title: COUNT in a scalar
debug.broken: SELECT name, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM enrollments) AS courses FROM students;
debug.fix: SELECT s.name, (SELECT COUNT(*) FROM enrollments e WHERE e.student_id = s.id) AS courses FROM students s;
debug.error: Every row shows the total count, not the per-student count

debug.title: DML CTE without RETURNING
debug.broken: WITH deleted AS (DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60) SELECT * FROM deleted;
debug.fix: WITH deleted AS (DELETE FROM students WHERE marks < 60 RETURNING *) SELECT * FROM deleted;
debug.error: WITH query "deleted" does not have a RETURNING clause

Membership in a multi-row subquery result.
Testing whether the subquery returns any row.

A named subquery defined with WITH.
